pageData.title: The Viceroyalty of New Granada
pageData.para1: The Viceroyalty of New Granada was a Spanish colony covering modern Colombia, Ecuador, Panama, and Venezuela. It was established in 1717 and centered on Bogotá. It produced gold, tobacco, and textiles.
pageData.para2: It became a center of independence movements led by Simón Bolívar. Gran Colombia was formed from its territories in 1819. It later split into separate nations.

pageData.title: The Viceroyalty of Río de la Plata
pageData.para1: The Viceroyalty of Río de la Plata was a Spanish colony covering modern Argentina, Uruguay, Paraguay, and Bolivia. It was created in 1776 with its capital at Buenos Aires. It was important for silver from Potosí and cattle products.
pageData.para2: It broke away during the Napoleonic wars. The May Revolution of 1810 began independence. It then fragmented into several countries.

pageData.title: Colonial Brazil
pageData.para1: Colonial Brazil was Portugal's largest and wealthiest colony. It was built on sugar plantations, gold mining, and enslaved African labor. The capital was Salvador and later Rio de Janeiro. It was ruled by a Portuguese governor-general and later a viceroy.
pageData.para2: Brazil became the center of the Portuguese empire when the royal family fled there in 1808. It declared independence in 1822 as an empire. It was the only Latin American monarchy.

pageData.title: Gran Colombia
pageData.para1: Gran Colombia was a short-lived republic created in 1819 by Simón Bolívar. It united modern Colombia, Venezuela, Ecuador, and Panama. It aimed to keep Spanish American independence strong through unity.
pageData.para2: Regional rivalries and political differences broke it apart by 1831. It split into Colombia, Venezuela, and Ecuador. Panama later became independent in 1903.

pageData.title: The Viceroyalty of Peru
pageData.para1: The Viceroyalty of Peru. The Viceroyalty of Peru was a major Spanish colonial administrative unit established in 1542, initially encompassing almost all of Spanish-controlled South America. Centered around its wealthy capital at Lima, the "City of the Kings," this administration matters because it served as the political and economic heart of Spain's South American empire for nearly three centuries, driven by the colossal silver production of the Potosí mines.
pageData.para2: The colonial economy relied heavily on the forced labor of indigenous populations through the adapted mita system, resulting in devastating human loss and repeated indigenous rebellions, most notably led by Túpac Amaru II in 1780. To improve administrative efficiency, the Spanish Crown later split off the Viceroyalties of New Granada and Río de la Plata in the 18th century. Lima remained a conservative royalist stronghold until liberating armies led by José de San Martín and Simón Bolívar finally secured independence in the 1820s.

pageData.title: The Spanish American Wars of Independence
pageData.para1: The Spanish American Wars of Independence. The Spanish American Wars of Independence were a series of revolutionary armed conflicts fought across Spanish America between 1808 and 1826, resulting in the creation of several independent nations. Triggered by the Napoleonic invasion of Spain and the deposition of King Ferdinand VII, local juntas formed across South America to claim self-governance. This era is historically momentous because it completely dismantled Spain's continental empire in the Americas.
pageData.para2: Brilliant military commanders like Simón Bolívar in the north and José de San Martín in the south led insurgent armies across harsh Andean terrain to defeat royalist forces. Key battles like Boyacá, Carabobo, and Ayacucho secured sovereignty for regions that became Gran Colombia, Peru, Chile, and Argentina. However, the newly formed republics were quickly plagued by territorial fragmentation, economic devastation, and political instability dominated by regional military strongmen (caudillos).

pageData.title: The Empire of Brazil
pageData.para1: The Empire of Brazil. The Empire of Brazil was a 19th-century state that encompassed modern-day Brazil, existing from 1822 to 1889 under the rule of Emperors Pedro I and Pedro II. Uniquely in Latin America, Brazil transitioned to independence without a prolonged, devastating war, as the Portuguese prince regent declared independence from Portugal and established a constitutional monarchy. This empire matters because it maintained territorial integrity and political stability across a massive landmass while neighboring Spanish-American republics fragmented.
pageData.para2: The empire operated a plantation economy heavily reliant on enslaved African labor to produce major cash crops like sugar and coffee. Emperor Pedro II oversaw decades of industrial modernization, cultural development, and relative political calm. However, the gradual abolition of slavery, culminating in the Golden Law of 1888, deeply alienated wealthy conservative coffee planters. Deprived of elite landlord support, the monarchy was overthrown in an unbloody military coup in 1889, establishing the First Brazilian Republic.
